item.title: Subclinical Left Ventricular Hypertrophy Among Emergency Department Patients With Elevated Blood Pressure
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: Hypertension (HTN) is a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, yet early detection of target organ damage is often missed, particularly in patients with limited access to care. The Emergency Department (ED), a key site of care for underserved populations, may offer an opportunity for risk stratification; we sought to determine the prevalence of LVH-a marker of subclinical disease and increased cardiovascular risk-among ED patients with asymptomatic elevated blood pressure and assess differences by sex, race, and insurance status.

Methods: We enrolled a convenience sample of adults aged 18-65 years presenting to an academic ED with blood pressure ≥ 140 mmHg systolic or ≥ 90 mmHg diastolic on two measurements. Subjects with prior LVH, active cardiac disease, hypertensive emergency, dialysis dependence, or pregnancy were excluded. LVH was identified using left ventricular mass indexed to height2.7 or body surface area via focused (point-of-care) cardiac ultrasound (parasternal long-axis view). Multivariate logistic regression assessed associations with LVH.

Results: Among 155 subjects, 46 (29.7%, 95% CI 22.5%-36.9%) had LVH. Mean age was 46.9 ± 12.1 years; 53.6% were women. LVH was more prevalent in women (38.6% vs. 19.4%; p = 0.009) and remained independently associated with female sex (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.14-5.22, p = 0.021) and prior hypertension (OR 2.47, 95% CI 1.14-5.39, p = 0.023). Notably, 18.3% of patients without a prior hypertension diagnosis demonstrated LVH (p = 0.004).

Conclusion: Nearly one-third of ED patients with elevated blood pressure had LVH, including many without known hypertension, with a higher prevalence among women.

Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05730309.

Baloescu C, Hesami M, Denkewicz R, Dziura J, McNamara R, Safdar B
